text.7-9: Matthew worked as a tax collector in Capernaum, and he collected money for the Roman government. Many people thought tax collectors were cheats. Jesus saw Matthew at his table and said, 'Follow me.' Matthew got up and followed him. Later Jesus was at dinner at Matthew's house, with many tax collectors and sinners. The Pharisees asked his disciples, 'Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?' Jesus heard it and said, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. I came to call sinners, not the righteous.'
text.10-12: Jesus goes where no one else wants to go. He sits down at a table with people whom others shun. The call to Matthew is only two words, 'Follow me'. And Matthew does not hesitate; he leaves his table and the money. Jesus uses the picture of a doctor, because people who are sick need help. This does not mean that people who feel good about themselves do not need him. It means that those who know their need are ready for him. Matthew later wrote the Gospel that bears his name. The Church honours him as an apostle and an evangelist on 21 September.

talk: What did Matthew do when Jesus called him?
Why did Jesus eat with tax collectors?
Who might you invite to sit with you?
stories.prayer: Jesus, thank you for calling me by name. Amen.

vocab.means: a person who collected money for the government

stories.title: The Soldier Who Believed

text.4-6: A Roman officer in Capernaum had a servant who was very ill. He loved his servant and asked Jesus for help. Jesus said, 'I will come and heal him.' The officer said, 'I am not good enough to have you in my house. Just say the word, and my servant will be well.' Jesus was amazed. He said, 'I have not seen such great faith.' The servant was healed that very hour.
text.7-9: A centurion, a Roman officer in charge of one hundred soldiers, came to Jesus in Capernaum. 'Lord, my servant is lying at home, paralysed and in great pain.' Jesus said, 'I will come and heal him.' The centurion answered, 'Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. But only say the word, and my servant will be healed. I am under authority, and I give orders and people do what I say.' Jesus was amazed and said to those following him, 'I have not found such faith in anyone in Israel.' Then Jesus said to the centurion, 'Go. Let it be done for you as you have believed.' The servant was healed at that very moment.
text.10-12: The centurion is a foreigner, and he is part of the army that rules Israel. Yet he cares for a servant, which was unusual at that time, and he shows more trust than many people who knew the Scriptures. He understands authority: when Jesus speaks, things happen. His words, 'Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof', are said by Catholics at every Mass before Communion. The humility of the centurion has become a prayer: 'but only say the word and I shall be healed.' Jesus says that people will come from east and west to the great feast, which means God's family is wide open.

talk: What did the officer believe about Jesus?
Why do you think Jesus was amazed?
Where do you hear the officer's words at Mass?
stories.prayer: Lord, I am not worthy, but only say the word and I shall be healed. Amen.

vocab.means: a Roman army officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers

stories.title: Jairus's Daughter

text.4-6: Jairus was an important man. His little girl was very ill. He begged Jesus, 'Please come!' On the way, a woman who had been ill for twelve years touched Jesus's cloak. She was healed. Then people came and said, 'Your daughter has died.' Jesus said, 'Do not be afraid. Just believe.' He took the girl's hand and said, 'Little girl, get up!' She stood up and walked. Jesus said, 'Give her something to eat.'
text.7-9: Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, fell at Jesus's feet and said, 'My little daughter is dying. Please come and lay your hands on her.' Jesus went with him. In the crowd a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years touched his cloak, thinking, 'If I just touch his clothes, I will be well.' Jesus felt power go out of him and asked who had touched him. She told him the whole truth. He said, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well.' Then people from Jairus's house said his daughter had died. Jesus said, 'Do not be afraid. Only believe.' He took the girl by the hand and said, 'Talitha koum', which means, 'Little girl, get up.' She got up and walked. He told them to give her something to eat.
text.10-12: Two stories are woven into one. Both end with a woman or girl called 'daughter', and the number twelve is in both: the girl is twelve, and the woman has been ill for twelve years. Jesus stops for the woman even though a child is dying, and he does not make Jairus feel that his need is less urgent. When he tells Jairus not to be afraid, he asks for faith in the worst moment. The Aramaic words are in the Gospel because the early Christians remembered how Jesus spoke. And he asks that they give her food. Jesus cares about the ordinary needs of a child who has just come back to life.

talk: What did the woman do when she touched Jesus's cloak?
What did Jesus say to Jairus?
Why do you think Jesus asked for food for the girl?
stories.prayer: Jesus, you are kind to everyone who needs you. Help me to trust you. Amen.

vocab.means: a place where Jewish people meet to pray and read

stories.title: The Widow's Son at Nain

text.4-6: Jesus came to a town called Nain. A funeral was coming out of the gate. A woman was crying because her only son had died. Jesus felt sorry for her. He said, 'Do not cry.' He touched the coffin and said, 'Young man, get up!' The young man sat up and began to talk. Jesus gave him back to his mother. The people said, 'God has visited his people!'
text.7-9: As Jesus came near the town of Nain, a dead man was being carried out. He was the only son of a woman who was already a widow, and a large crowd from the town was with her. When the Lord saw her, his heart went out to her. He said, 'Do not weep.' Then he went up and touched the open coffin, and the bearers stood still. 'Young man,' he said, 'I tell you, get up!' The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. Fear came on everyone, and they praised God and said, 'A great prophet has risen among us. God has visited his people.'
text.10-12: Nobody asks Jesus to do anything in this story. He sees a woman who has lost her husband and now her son, and has no one left to look after her. That was a very dangerous place for a woman in that time. Jesus acts out of compassion, which means he suffers with her. He touches the coffin, which a Jew was not supposed to do, and he commands death to let go. The story echoes the earlier one about Elijah and the widow's son. The Gospel of Luke says 'the Lord' here, a word that hints at who Jesus really is. It is a gift for anyone who has lost someone.

talk: Why did Jesus feel sorry for the woman?
What did Jesus say to the young man?
How can you comfort a person who is sad?
stories.prayer: Jesus, comfort everyone who is sad today. Amen.

vocab.means: the box in which a person who has died is carried

stories.title: Jesus Opens a Man's Ears

text.4-6: Some friends brought a man who could not hear or talk well. They begged Jesus to help him. Jesus took the man aside, away from the crowd. He touched the man's ears and tongue. He looked up to heaven and said, 'Ephphatha!' That means, 'Be opened!' The man could hear and talk! The people were amazed. They said, 'He does everything well!'
text.7-9: Some people brought to Jesus a man who was deaf and could hardly speak. They asked Jesus to lay his hand on him. Jesus took the man away from the crowd, privately. He put his fingers into the man's ears, and then touched his tongue. Looking up to heaven, he sighed and said, 'Ephphatha', which means, 'Be opened.' At once the man's ears were opened, his tongue was freed, and he spoke plainly. Jesus told the people not to tell anyone, but the more he told them, the more they spread the news. They were astonished and said, 'He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.'
text.10-12: Jesus takes the man away from the crowd, and he treats him gently. A man who cannot hear or speak would have felt very alone, and Jesus uses touch to say, 'I am with you.' The word 'Ephphatha' stayed in the Gospel in the language Jesus spoke. In the Baptism liturgy, the priest touches the ears and mouth of the baby and prays that he or she may listen to the word of God and speak the faith. That ritual comes straight from this story. The crowd's words, 'He has done all things well', echo the creation story where God sees that everything he made is good.

talk: How did Jesus help the man?
Why do you think Jesus took him away from the crowd?
What would you like to hear God say to you today?
stories.prayer: Lord, open my ears to hear you and my mouth to praise you. Amen.

vocab.means: a word Jesus spoke in his own language, meaning 'Be opened'

stories.title: The Man Who Was Born Blind

text.4-6: A man had been blind from birth. Jesus made a little mud with his spit and put it on the man's eyes. 'Go and wash in the pool of Siloam,' he said. The man went, washed, and could see! His neighbours asked, 'Is this the same man?' He said, 'Yes. I was blind, and now I see.' Later Jesus found him and said, 'Do you believe?' The man said, 'Lord, I believe.'
text.7-9: As Jesus walked along, he saw a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked whose fault it was. Jesus said, 'It was not that this man sinned, or his parents. This happened so that God's works might be shown in him.' Jesus put mud on the man's eyes and told him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. He went and washed and came back seeing. His neighbours could hardly believe it, and the leaders questioned him again and again. His parents were afraid to say much. The man said simply, 'One thing I do know. I was blind, and now I see.' Later Jesus found him and said, 'Do you believe in the Son of Man?' He answered, 'Lord, I believe,' and worshipped him.
text.10-12: Everyone in this story has a lot to say except the man himself, who keeps to the plain truth. He does not know all the answers about who Jesus is. He knows what happened to him. As he is asked more questions, his belief grows from 'the man called Jesus' to 'a prophet' to 'Lord, I believe'. The leaders, who think they can see, are the ones who cannot. The Church reads this story in Lent and uses it for baptism, because baptism was called 'enlightenment'. The story also teaches that illness is not a punishment for someone's sin.

talk: What did the man say again and again when people asked him questions?
Who could not see in this story, even though they had good eyes?
What has Jesus helped you to see?
stories.prayer: Jesus, light of the world, help me to see clearly. Amen.

vocab.means: a pool in Jerusalem; the name means 'sent'

stories.title: Jesus Shines Like the Sun

text.4-6: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain. Suddenly Jesus shone. His face was bright as the sun, and his clothes were white as light. Moses and Elijah were there, talking with him. A bright cloud came, and a voice said, 'This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!' The friends were scared. Jesus touched them and said, 'Get up. Do not be afraid.'
text.7-9: Six days after Peter said that Jesus was the Messiah, Jesus led Peter, James and John up a high mountain by themselves. There he was changed in front of them. His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as light. Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with him. Peter said, 'Lord, it is good for us to be here. Let me make three shelters.' While he was speaking, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice from the cloud said, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.' The disciples fell on their faces, terrified. Jesus came and touched them and said, 'Get up, and do not be afraid.' When they looked up, they saw only Jesus.
text.10-12: Jesus knew that hard days were coming, and he gave three of his friends a glimpse of who he really was. Moses stands for the Law and Elijah for the prophets. Together, they show that the whole Old Testament points to Jesus. The voice from the cloud sounds like the voice at his baptism, and it adds one command: 'Listen to him.' Peter wants to stay on the mountain, but they have to go down, back to the road that leads to Jerusalem. The Church celebrates the Transfiguration on 6 August. It reminds us that God's glory is behind the ordinary face of Jesus.

talk: Who appeared with Jesus on the mountain?
What did the voice from the cloud say?
What does it mean to listen to Jesus?
stories.prayer: Jesus, help me to listen to you every day. Amen.

vocab.means: changed in a wonderful way

stories.title: The Good Shepherd

text.4-6: Jesus said, 'I am the Good Shepherd. A good shepherd knows his sheep by name. The sheep know his voice. They follow him because they trust him. A strange voice they would never follow. I know my sheep, and they know me. I love them so much that I will give my life for them.'
text.7-9: Jesus told the people a story about sheep. A shepherd goes in by the door, and the sheep recognise his voice. He calls each one by name and leads them out. They will not follow a stranger, because they do not know his voice. Then Jesus said, 'I am the door of the sheep. Whoever enters by me will be saved.' He said, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. A hired hand, who is not a shepherd, runs away when he sees a wolf coming. But I know my sheep and my sheep know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father. And there are other sheep too, and they will hear my voice. There will be one flock, one shepherd.'
text.10-12: Shepherds in Israel knew every sheep by name, and Jesus's hearers would have understood at once. He says two things about himself: he is the door, and he is the shepherd. A door protects and lets in. A shepherd knows and leads. The hired hand is the one who works for pay and cares more about himself. The good shepherd gives his life, which points ahead to the cross. When he says 'other sheep', he means that people from every nation will be gathered. The image of Jesus as the Good Shepherd was one of the earliest in Christian art, painted on the walls of the catacombs.

talk: How does the shepherd know his sheep?
What does the good shepherd do for his sheep?
How can you hear Jesus's voice?
stories.prayer: Jesus, my shepherd, thank you for knowing me and loving me. Amen.

vocab.means: someone paid to look after sheep, who may run away from danger

stories.title: The House on the Rock

text.4-6: Jesus told a story about two builders. One built his house on a rock. The rain fell, the floods came, and the wind blew. The house did not fall. The other built his house on sand. When the storm came, that house fell with a great crash. Jesus said, 'The wise one hears my words and does them.'
text.7-9: At the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus told this story. 'Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain came down, the floods rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, but it did not fall, because it was founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them is like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew, and that house fell, and great was its fall.' The crowds were amazed at his teaching.
text.10-12: The two houses look the same until the storm hits. The difference is under the ground, where no one can see. The wise builder is not smarter or luckier. He hears Jesus and does what Jesus says. That is all. Jesus does not promise that there will be no storms. The same wind and water hit both houses. But a life built on his words can stand. A song about this story is one of the first that many children learn. It is a story for grown-ups too, because Jesus asked for action, not just good intentions.

talk: What is the difference between the two houses?
What does it mean to build on the rock?
What is one thing Jesus asked us to do that you can do today?
stories.prayer: Lord, help me to hear your words and to do them. Amen.

vocab.means: the base a house is built on

stories.title: Look at the Birds

text.4-6: Jesus said, 'Do not worry about what you will eat or wear. Look at the birds. They do not plant seeds or fill barns, but God feeds them. And you are worth more than birds! Look at the wild flowers. They do not work, but God makes them beautiful. So do not worry. Your Father knows what you need.'
text.7-9: Jesus told the crowd, 'Do not worry about your life, about what you will eat or drink, or what you will wear. Is life not more than food, and the body more than clothes? Look at the birds in the sky. They do not sow or reap or store in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they? And why do you worry about clothes? See how the lilies of the field grow. They do not work or spin. Yet not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of these. Seek first God's kingdom, and everything else will be given to you. Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will take care of itself.'
text.10-12: Jesus is not saying that we should be careless. Birds work hard to find food, and flowers have to grow. He is saying that worry does not add a single hour to life, and that God cares. Being worried is natural, and Jesus takes it seriously. His answer is to look out of the window. The birds and flowers are a picture of how God looks after everything he made. The command to 'seek first his kingdom' puts God in the first place, and trusts that the rest will follow. 'Give us this day our daily bread' in the Our Father is the same trust, in a prayer.

talk: What did Jesus say about the birds?
What worries you?
What can you do when you feel worried?
stories.prayer: Father, you take care of me. Help me not to be afraid. Amen.

vocab.means: wild flowers that grow in the fields

stories.title: The Hidden Treasure

text.4-6: Jesus told two short stories. A man found treasure hidden in a field. He was so happy that he sold everything he had to buy that field. A trader found one beautiful pearl. It was more valuable than all his other pearls. He sold everything and bought it. Jesus said, 'God's kingdom is like this.'
text.7-9: Jesus said, 'The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. A man found it and hid it again, and in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field.' Then he said, 'The kingdom of heaven is also like a merchant looking for fine pearls. When he found one of great price, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it.' The stories are short and they are very much alike. In both, someone finds something so good that nothing else compares, and gives everything for it. Both are done with joy.
text.10-12: These stories do not say that God's kingdom is hard to get. They say it is wonderful. The man in the first story did not find it by looking, and the merchant in the second spent a lifetime searching. People find Jesus in different ways. What they have in common is that when they see how good he is, everything else seems small. The word 'joy' in the first story is important. Nobody has to be forced. In the Church, some people give up many things to follow Jesus, such as monks and sisters. But all of us can ask what is the treasure in our lives.

talk: What did the man in the first story do when he found the treasure?
Why did the merchant sell everything?
What is the most precious thing in your life?
stories.prayer: Jesus, you are my treasure. Help me to love you most of all. Amen.

vocab.means: a person who buys and sells goods

stories.title: The Friend at Midnight

text.4-6: Jesus told a story. A man's friend arrived at midnight and he had no bread. So he knocked on his neighbour's door. 'Please lend me three loaves!' The neighbour said, 'Go away, I am in bed.' But the man kept knocking. At last the neighbour got up and gave him the bread. Jesus said, 'Keep asking. Keep knocking. Your Father in heaven loves to give good gifts.'
text.7-9: After teaching his friends the Our Father, Jesus told them another story about prayer. 'Suppose one of you has a friend, and you go to him at midnight and say, Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has just arrived and I have nothing to give him. And he answers from inside, Do not bother me. The door is locked and the children are in bed with me. I cannot get up. I tell you, even if he will not get up because you are his friend, he will get up and give you what you need because you are so bold.' Then Jesus said, 'Ask, and it will be given. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened to you.'
text.10-12: The neighbour in the story is grumpy, and God is not. The story says: if even a tired neighbour finally gives, how much more will your Father in heaven give? Jesus follows it with another picture. No father would give his child a snake when the child asks for a fish. The best gift God gives is the Holy Spirit. Persistence in prayer means not giving up, and it also means trusting that God is listening. We may not get what we ask for in the way we expect, but we are heard, and God gives what is good for us.

talk: Why did the man keep knocking?
What does Jesus say about God's gifts?
Is there something you keep praying about?
stories.prayer: Father, thank you that you listen. Help me to keep praying. Amen.

vocab.means: not giving up

stories.title: Two Men Who Prayed

text.4-6: Two men went to the Temple to pray. One was a Pharisee. He stood tall and said, 'God, thank you that I am better than other people!' The other man was a tax collector. He stood far away and did not even look up. He said, 'God, be kind to me. I have done wrong.' Jesus said, 'The second man went home friends with God.'
text.7-9: Jesus told this story to some people who were sure of their own goodness and looked down on others. 'Two men went up to the Temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed, God, I thank you that I am not like other people, greedy, dishonest, or like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give a tenth of all I get. But the tax collector stood far off. He would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast and said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner. I tell you, this man went home justified rather than the other. Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
text.10-12: The Pharisee's prayer is not about God. It is about himself and how well he compares with other people. He does good things, and Jesus does not say the things are bad. He says that the Pharisee's heart is closed. The tax collector's prayer is short and honest. 'Lord, have mercy' is a prayer that many Christians have prayed over and over. It is the Jesus Prayer of the Eastern Churches, and it is the 'Lord, have mercy' of the Mass. God does not look for perfect people. He looks for people who are willing to be honest with him.

talk: How did the two men pray differently?
Which prayer did God like?
What do you say to God when you have done something wrong?
stories.prayer: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Amen.

vocab.means: a member of a group of Jews who tried very carefully to keep the law

stories.title: The Servant Who Would Not Forgive

text.4-6: Peter asked Jesus, 'How many times must I forgive someone? Seven times?' Jesus said, 'Not seven, but seventy times seven!' Then he told a story. A king forgave a servant a huge debt. But that servant would not forgive a friend who owed him a little. The king said, 'I forgave you a lot. Should you not forgive a little?' Jesus said, 'Forgive from your heart.'
text.7-9: Peter asked Jesus how often he had to forgive a brother, and he suggested seven times. Jesus answered, 'Seventy times seven.' Then he told the story of a king whose servant owed him a huge amount, ten thousand talents. The servant begged for time, and the king felt sorry for him and cancelled the whole debt. But as that servant left, he met a fellow servant who owed him a few coins. He grabbed him by the throat and had him put in prison. When the king heard, he called the first servant and said, 'I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Should you not have shown mercy as I showed mercy to you?' Jesus said, 'So my heavenly Father will do to you, unless you forgive your brother from your heart.'
text.10-12: Seventy times seven does not mean that we should count to 490 and stop. It means that forgiveness should not run out. The first debt is far too big to pay back. That is how much God forgives us. The second debt is small. The point of the story is that people who have been forgiven so much should be glad to forgive. We say the same in the Our Father: 'Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.' This does not mean we pretend that no one hurt us. It means we let go of the wish to pay them back.

talk: How much did the king forgive?
Why was the king upset?
Who do you need to forgive?
stories.prayer: Father, forgive me as I forgive others. Amen.

vocab.means: money or something else that you owe

stories.title: The Ten Girls and Their Lamps

text.4-6: Jesus told a story about ten girls waiting for a wedding. They each had a lamp. Five took extra oil with them. Five did not. The groom was late, and they all fell asleep. At midnight a shout came: 'He is coming!' The wise girls' lamps were ready. The others had no oil. They ran to buy some, but the door was shut when they came back. Jesus said, 'Be ready.'
text.7-9: Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is like ten bridesmaids who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish and five were wise. The foolish ones took their lamps but no oil. The wise ones took flasks of oil with their lamps. The bridegroom was a long time coming, and they all became drowsy and slept. At midnight there was a shout: 'Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!' The foolish asked the wise for oil, but the wise said there would not be enough for everyone. While the foolish ones were gone, the bridegroom came, and the door was shut. Jesus ended, 'Keep awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour.'
text.10-12: This is a story of being ready, and it is often read in the last weeks of the Church's year. All ten fall asleep. The difference is not that the wise ones were awake and the others sleepy. It is that the wise ones prepared. The oil is often taken to mean a life of prayer and kindness, which cannot be borrowed at the last minute. The wedding feast is a picture of life with God. Jesus is not trying to frighten anyone. He wants us to live well each day, so that when he comes, we are glad to see him.

talk: What was different about the wise girls?
What do you think the oil stands for?
What can you do every day to be ready?
stories.prayer: Jesus, keep me ready for you. Amen.

vocab.means: a man who is about to be married

stories.title: Breakfast by the Lake

text.4-6: Peter and his friends fished all night and caught nothing. In the morning a man on the shore called, 'Throw your net on the right side!' They did, and the net was so full of fish they could not pull it in. John said, 'It is the Lord!' Peter jumped into the water and swam to shore. Jesus had a fire and bread and fish ready. He said, 'Come and eat.'
text.7-9: After the resurrection, seven of the disciples went fishing on the Sea of Galilee, and they caught nothing all night. At dawn Jesus stood on the shore, though they did not recognise him. He called, 'Have you any fish?' When they said no, he told them to cast the net on the right side of the boat. It was so full that they could not haul it in. John said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!' Peter jumped into the sea. When they landed, there was a charcoal fire with fish and bread on it. They counted a hundred and fifty-three fish, and the net was not torn. Jesus said, 'Come and have breakfast.'
text.10-12: Peter had said three times that he did not know Jesus. Now there is a charcoal fire again. Jesus asks Peter three times, 'Do you love me?' And three times Peter says yes. Each time Jesus gives him a job: 'Feed my lambs. Look after my sheep.' It is a gentle way of healing a wound. The story is full of small details: the count of the fish, the fire, the bread. These are things someone remembered because they were there. Jesus does not scold Peter. He makes breakfast, and he gives Peter the work of caring for the Church.

talk: What did the disciples find when they threw the net on the other side?
Why did Jesus ask Peter the same question three times?
What does it mean to feed Jesus's sheep?
stories.prayer: Jesus, you know that I love you. Help me to follow you. Amen.

stories.title: Thomas Sees Jesus

text.4-6: On Easter evening the friends of Jesus were together in a room with the doors locked. Jesus came and said, 'Peace be with you!' But Thomas was not there. When they told him, he said, 'I will not believe until I see.' A week later, Jesus came again. 'Thomas, touch my hands,' he said. Thomas said, 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus said, 'Happy are those who believe without seeing.'
text.7-9: On the evening of the first Easter, the disciples were hiding behind locked doors because they were afraid. Suddenly Jesus was standing among them. He said, 'Peace be with you.' He showed them his hands and his side, and they were filled with joy. Thomas was not there. When they told him, 'We have seen the Lord,' he said, 'Unless I see the marks of the nails in his hands, I will not believe.' A week later they were together again, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and said, 'Peace be with you.' He said to Thomas, 'Put your finger here and see my hands.' Thomas answered, 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus said, 'Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe.'
text.10-12: Thomas is often called 'doubting Thomas', but he asks for what the others had already received. He wants to see Jesus. When he does, he says the strongest words of faith in the Gospel: 'My Lord and my God.' Nobody in the Gospel says this before. Jesus does not scold Thomas. He comes back for him. His last words are for the rest of us, who have not seen him with our eyes. The Church reads this Gospel on the Sunday after Easter, which is now called Divine Mercy Sunday. We believe through the witness of those who did see.

talk: Why did Thomas want to see Jesus's hands?
What did Thomas say when he saw Jesus?
What helps you to believe?
stories.prayer: My Lord and my God! Amen.

stories.title: Jesus Goes Up to Heaven

text.4-6: For forty days after Easter, Jesus was with his friends. Then he told them to wait in Jerusalem. 'You will receive power from the Holy Spirit. You will tell people about me all over the world.' As they watched, Jesus was lifted up, and a cloud hid him from sight. Two men in white said, 'Why do you stand looking at the sky? Jesus will come back in the same way.'
text.7-9: After his resurrection, Jesus appeared to his disciples many times over forty days and spoke to them about the kingdom of God. He told them not to leave Jerusalem. 'Wait for the gift my Father promised. John baptised with water, but you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit in a few days.' They asked, 'Lord, will you now restore the kingdom to Israel?' Jesus said, 'It is not for you to know the times. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.' As they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. Two men in white stood beside them and said, 'This Jesus will come back in the same way you saw him go.'
text.10-12: The disciples keep looking at the sky, and the angels gently turn them around. The task is here on earth. Jesus goes to the Father, and his friends are to stay, wait, pray, and then go out. The words 'to the ends of the earth' are the outline of the book of Acts, as the good news spreads from Jerusalem to Rome. Jesus does not leave them alone. He promises the Holy Spirit. The Church celebrates the Ascension forty days after Easter. At every Mass, Catholics say, 'He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.'

talk: What did Jesus tell his friends to wait for?
Why did the two men ask the disciples why they were looking at the sky?
How can you be a witness for Jesus?
stories.prayer: Jesus, thank you that you are with the Father and with us. Amen.

vocab.means: a person who tells what they have seen and heard

stories.title: The Vine and the Branches

text.4-6: Jesus said, 'I am the vine and you are the branches. A branch cannot grow grapes on its own. It must stay joined to the vine. If you stay close to me, you will bear much fruit. Love one another, as I have loved you.'
text.7-9: At the Last Supper, Jesus said to his friends, 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener. Every branch in me that bears no fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, so that it will bear more fruit. Remain in me, as I remain in you. No branch can bear fruit by itself, it must stay in the vine. Neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. If you remain in me and I in you, you will bear much fruit, for without me you can do nothing.' Then he said, 'This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.'
text.10-12: The vine was an image often used for Israel in the Old Testament. Jesus now says that he is the true vine. A branch is useful only when it stays attached to the vine. It has no life of its own. This is a picture of prayer, the sacraments and a life joined to Jesus. 'Pruning' sounds painful, but it helps the plant grow. The fruit is love, and Jesus is clear about what that means. It is staying with him and loving the people he loves, even when it costs something. At Mass, the wine is a sign of this vine.

talk: What does the branch need?
What is the fruit that Jesus talks about?
How can you stay close to Jesus?
stories.prayer: Jesus, help me to stay close to you. Amen.

vocab.means: to cut back a plant so it grows better

stories.title: The Song of Love

text.4-6: Saint Paul wrote a letter about love. He said that love is patient and kind. Love is not jealous or proud. Love does not give up. Even if I could do wonderful things, but have no love, I am like a noisy gong. Faith, hope and love will last forever. The greatest of these is love.
text.7-9: Saint Paul wrote to the Christians in Corinth about what matters most. 'If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have no love, I am only a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. If I give all I have to the poor, but have no love, it gains me nothing. Love is patient. Love is kind. Love is not jealous, it does not brag, it is not proud. It does not insist on its own way. It is not irritable, it does not keep a record of wrongs. It is not glad about injustice but is glad about the truth. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.' He ended: 'Now faith, hope and love remain, these three. The greatest of these is love.'
text.10-12: The Corinthian Church had many gifts and many quarrels. Paul reminds them that gifts without love are noise. He then describes love by what it does, not by what it feels. This is why the passage is read at so many weddings. It is not only for husbands and wives. It describes how God loves us, and how we are asked to love one another. The line 'It does not keep a record of wrongs' can be hard to practise. And Paul says that when we see God face to face, faith and hope will be fulfilled, but love will remain forever.

talk: What does Paul say love is like?
Which part of love is hardest for you?
How can you show love this week?
stories.prayer: God, you are love. Teach me to love like you. Amen.

vocab.means: a large metal disc that makes a loud sound when struck

stories.title: Peter and the Man at the Gate

text.4-6: Peter and John went to the Temple to pray. A man who could not walk sat by the gate, begging. He asked them for money. Peter said, 'I have no silver or gold. But I will give you what I have. In the name of Jesus, stand up and walk!' Peter took his hand and helped him up. The man jumped, walked and praised God!
text.7-9: At three in the afternoon, Peter and John were going up to the Temple to pray. At the gate called Beautiful sat a man who had been lame since birth. Every day he was carried there to beg. He asked Peter and John for money. Peter looked straight at him and said, 'Look at us.' The man looked, expecting a gift. Peter said, 'I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.' He took the man by the right hand and raised him up. At once his feet and ankles were made strong. He leaped up, stood, walked, and went into the Temple with them, walking and jumping and praising God.
text.10-12: The man asks for a small coin, and he gets far more. Peter first looks at him, which beggars are not used to. Then he gives him what he really has, which is the name of Jesus. The healing is not Peter's own power. He says so plainly in the verses that follow. What is most striking is the man's response. He does not run off. He goes into the Temple praising God, and everyone who knew him as a beggar sees him walk. The Church has always taken from this story that the best gift we can give is Jesus himself, along with whatever help we can offer.

talk: What did the man ask for?
What did Peter give him?
What can you give to someone, other than money?
stories.prayer: Jesus, help me to look at people and to share what I have. Amen.

stories.title: The First Christians Share

text.4-6: After Pentecost, many people believed in Jesus. They met together to pray and to hear the apostles. They broke bread together. They shared everything they had. If someone was in need, others gave to help. They were happy, and they praised God. Every day, more people joined them.
text.7-9: After Pentecost, the believers spent time listening to the apostles, sharing meals, breaking bread and praying together. Many wonders were done by the apostles. All who believed were together and had everything in common. They sold their property and goods and gave the money to anyone who had need. Day by day they went to the Temple together and broke bread in their homes, eating with glad and generous hearts, praising God. The Bible says there were no needy persons among them, because those who owned land or houses sold them and brought the money to the apostles to be shared. And the Lord added to their number day by day.
text.10-12: This is a picture of what the early Church looked like. Four things are named: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread (the Eucharist) and prayer. The sharing is not forced; people give gladly because they love their neighbours. The people who joined were attracted by what they saw, not by a speech. Not every group of Christians has lived exactly this way, and the Acts of the Apostles also tells of problems. But it is a standard for all later Christians. Religious communities such as monasteries try to live it closely. Everyone can see how a parish can help the needy in practical ways.

talk: What four things did the first Christians do together?
How did they treat people who needed help?
How does your family or parish share?
stories.prayer: Lord, make us a family that shares and prays together. Amen.

vocab.means: friendship and sharing among people who believe the same thing

stories.title: Tabitha Gets Up

text.4-6: In the town of Joppa there lived a kind woman called Tabitha. She made clothes for the poor. One day she became ill and died. Her friends were very sad. They sent for Peter. When Peter came, the widows showed him the coats and clothes she had made. Peter prayed and said, 'Tabitha, get up!' She opened her eyes. Peter helped her up, and her friends were so happy.
text.7-9: In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which in Greek is Dorcas. She was always doing good and helping the poor. At that time she became ill and died, and her body was washed and laid in an upstairs room. The disciples had heard that Peter was nearby, so they sent two men to ask him to come at once. Peter went with them. The room was full of widows, crying and showing him the tunics and other clothes Tabitha had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out of the room, knelt down and prayed. Then he turned to the body and said, 'Tabitha, get up.' She opened her eyes, saw Peter, and sat up. He gave her his hand and helped her up, and he called the believers and widows and showed her to them alive.
text.10-12: Tabitha is the only woman in the New Testament who is called a 'disciple' by that word. Her work was practical. She sewed. The widows do not say what a good person she was. They show Peter the clothes. Her life is remembered by what she did for others. Peter's actions are much like Jesus's in the story of Jairus's daughter: he sends the crowd away, and he speaks to her by name. The story is not mostly about Peter's power. It is about a community that loved a woman and asked God to give her back. Many people in the town came to believe.

talk: What did Tabitha do for people?
What did the widows show Peter?
What useful thing can you make or do for someone?
stories.prayer: Lord, thank you for people who help in quiet ways. Help me to do the same. Amen.

vocab.means: a woman whose husband has died

stories.title: Peter and Cornelius

text.4-6: Cornelius was a Roman soldier who prayed to God and gave to the poor. An angel told him, 'Send for Peter.' Meanwhile, God showed Peter a vision of a big sheet full of animals. A voice said, 'Do not call anything unclean that God has made clean.' Then men from Cornelius came to Peter's door. Peter went with them. He told them about Jesus. While he was speaking, the Holy Spirit came on them all! Peter said, 'God has no favourites.'
text.7-9: Cornelius was a Roman officer in Caesarea. He was a good man who prayed and gave generously, though he was not Jewish. One afternoon an angel told him to send for a man named Peter. The next day, while Peter was praying on a rooftop in Joppa, he saw a vision of a large sheet coming down from heaven filled with all kinds of animals. A voice said, 'Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.' Peter said no, because some of the animals were forbidden by the law. The voice said, 'What God has made clean, you must not call unclean.' This happened three times. At that moment the men from Cornelius arrived. Peter went to the house, and said, 'God has shown me that I should not call anyone unclean.' As Peter spoke about Jesus, the Holy Spirit fell on all who were listening, and they were baptised.
text.10-12: This is one of the turning points in Acts. Until now almost all the followers of Jesus were Jewish. Peter, a Jew who followed the old food laws, would not normally enter the home of a Gentile. God had to teach him. The vision was not really about food. It was about people. Peter says, 'I truly understand that God shows no partiality.' When the Holy Spirit comes on the household of Cornelius just as at Pentecost, no one can say that they are not part of the Church. The story helps explain why the Church is open to every nation. It was a hard lesson for the early Christians, and Peter takes his time to learn it.

talk: What did God teach Peter through the vision?
What happened to Cornelius and his family?
Who might feel left out at your school or church, and how can you include them?
stories.prayer: Lord, thank you that everyone belongs to you. Help me to welcome everyone. Amen.

vocab.means: a person who is not Jewish

stories.title: Peter Escapes from Prison

text.4-6: King Herod put Peter in prison. The church prayed hard for him. In the night, an angel woke Peter. 'Get up quickly!' The chains fell off his hands. The angel led him past the guards, and the big iron gate opened by itself! Peter went to the house where his friends were praying. A girl called Rhoda heard his voice. She was so happy she forgot to open the door! She ran to tell everyone. At last they let Peter in, and they were amazed.
text.7-9: Herod arrested Peter and put him in prison, with four squads of soldiers to guard him. The church prayed to God for him earnestly. The night before the trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Suddenly an angel stood beside him and a light shone in the cell. The angel hit Peter on the side and said, 'Get up quickly.' The chains fell off. 'Put on your belt and sandals and follow me.' Peter thought he was dreaming. They passed the guards, and the iron gate opened by itself. Then the angel left. Peter went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many were praying. When the servant girl Rhoda heard his voice, she was so happy that she ran to tell the others instead of opening the gate. 'You are out of your mind,' they said. Peter kept knocking, and when they opened, they were amazed.
text.10-12: This story has some humour. The church was praying for Peter all night, and when he is at the door they cannot believe it. Rhoda is so glad that she forgets to open it. It is honest about how people pray: they do pray, and they also doubt. Peter, in a prison cell, is so calm that he is asleep. The angel has to nudge him. He tells them to 'tell this to James and the brothers' and goes to another place. The story shows that prayer is real and that God cares for his messengers. It is also a reminder that not every prisoner is freed in this way, and the Church prays for those who are in prison for their faith.

talk: What did the church do while Peter was in prison?
What happened when Rhoda heard Peter's voice?
Who would you like to pray for?
stories.prayer: Lord, thank you for hearing our prayers. Please look after people who are in prison or in danger. Amen.

vocab.means: a messenger sent by God

stories.title: Lydia Opens Her Home

text.4-6: Paul went to the city of Philippi. On the Sabbath he went to the river, where some women were praying. One of them was Lydia. She sold purple cloth. The Lord opened her heart to what Paul said about Jesus. She and her family were baptised. Then she said to Paul and his friends, 'If you think I belong to the Lord, please come and stay at my house.' And they did.
text.7-9: Paul and his companions sailed to Macedonia and came to Philippi, a Roman city. On the Sabbath they went outside the gate by the river, where they expected to find a place of prayer. They sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered. One of them was a woman called Lydia, a seller of purple cloth from the city of Thyatira. She worshipped God. The Lord opened her heart to listen to what Paul was saying. She and her household were baptised, and she invited them: 'If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come and stay at my house.' And she persuaded them.
text.10-12: Lydia is the first person in Europe in Acts to become a Christian, and it begins with women praying by a river. She is a businesswoman who sells expensive purple cloth, and she has a household. The Bible says that 'the Lord opened her heart', and that she then acted: she was baptised and offered her home. The house of Lydia later became a meeting place for the Church in Philippi. When Paul wrote to the Philippians, he said he thanked God for their partnership in the Gospel from the first day. Welcoming people into a home is one of the simplest and most lasting ways of serving God.

talk: Where did Paul find Lydia?
What did Lydia do after she was baptised?
How can your family welcome visitors?
stories.prayer: Lord, open my heart, and help me to open my home to others. Amen.

vocab.means: a city in Greece where Paul first preached in Europe

stories.title: The Boy Who Fell Asleep

text.4-6: Paul was visiting friends. He talked for a very long time, until midnight. A young man named Eutychus sat in a window. He was so sleepy that he fell asleep and fell out of the window! Everyone ran down. Paul hugged him and said, 'Do not worry. He is alive!' They took him home, and they were very glad. Paul kept on talking until morning.
text.7-9: On the first day of the week the Christians in Troas met to break bread. Paul talked with them, and since he was leaving the next day, he went on speaking until midnight. There were many lamps in the upstairs room. A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window. As Paul talked on and on, Eutychus sank into a deep sleep and fell from the third storey to the ground. He was picked up dead. But Paul went down, threw himself on him, put his arms around him and said, 'Do not be alarmed. His life is in him.' Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread and ate, and talked until dawn. They took the young man away alive, and they were greatly comforted.
text.10-12: This is one of the most down-to-earth stories in the Bible. It tells us that the early Christians met on Sunday, 'the first day of the week', to break bread. It also tells us they sat in a hot, crowded room with lots of lamps, and a young person fell asleep during a long talk. The story is gentle with Eutychus. Nobody blames him. Paul runs down and embraces him, as Elijah and Elisha had done for children in the Old Testament. Afterwards the community goes back upstairs and shares the Eucharist together. The Bible does not mind showing ordinary life in the Church.

talk: Why did Eutychus fall?
How did Paul act?
What would you do if a friend were hurt?
stories.prayer: Lord, thank you for watching over us when we are weak or tired. Amen.

stories.title: Paul in the Storm

text.4-6: Paul was on a ship going to Rome. A huge storm hit the ship. For many days nobody could see the sun or stars. The sailors were afraid. But an angel told Paul, 'Do not be afraid. God will save everyone on this ship.' Paul told the people, 'Eat some food. Be brave.' He thanked God for the bread. At last the ship ran aground near an island. Everyone got safely to land.
text.7-9: Paul was a prisoner on a ship bound for Rome, with 275 other people on board. A fierce wind struck, and for many days they could see neither sun nor stars. They threw cargo overboard, and finally gave up all hope. Paul stood up and said, 'An angel of the God to whom I belong stood by me last night and said, Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. God has given you the lives of all who sail with you.' After two weeks, Paul urged everyone to eat. He took bread, gave thanks to God in front of them all, broke it and began to eat. They were encouraged, and ate too. When day came, the ship ran aground and broke apart, but everyone made it to land, some swimming and some on pieces of the ship.
text.10-12: Paul is in chains, and yet he is the calm one on the ship. His calm comes from prayer and from what the angel has told him. He does not tell everyone that nothing will go wrong. He tells them that God will keep them all alive, and then he acts sensibly: he asks them to eat. The words he uses, taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it, sound very like the Last Supper. Luke, who wrote Acts, was on the ship, and tells it like an eyewitness, with many details. The story shows that God's promises and our ordinary work belong together.

talk: How did Paul help the people on the ship?
Why did Paul ask everyone to eat?
What helps you stay calm when you are afraid?
stories.prayer: Lord, be with me in every storm. Amen.

vocab.means: stuck on the bottom, when a ship hits land or sand

stories.title: Barnabas, the Encourager

text.4-6: A man named Joseph had a nickname: Barnabas. It means 'son of encouragement'. He sold a field and gave the money to the apostles. When Paul came to Jerusalem, everyone was afraid of him. Barnabas said, 'I will be his friend.' He brought Paul to the apostles and told them Paul was a new person. Later Barnabas went to Antioch, and he was very glad to see God's love there. He encouraged everyone.
text.7-9: The apostles gave Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, the name Barnabas, which means 'son of encouragement'. He sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet. After Saul, who later became Paul, was converted, he went to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples. But they were all afraid of him, since he had been a persecutor. Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and had spoken boldly in Damascus. Later the Church sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he encouraged all of them to remain faithful. He then went to find Saul, and brought him to Antioch. There the disciples were first called Christians.
text.10-12: Barnabas shows what a friend can do. He believes in Paul when no one else will, and he uses his own good name to say that Paul can be trusted. Without Barnabas, Paul might never have joined the Church in Jerusalem. Barnabas is generous with money, and generous with trust. He goes to Antioch and does not boss anyone. He sees good and encourages it. Then he invites Paul to work with him. Some of the best things in the Church begin with someone who simply says, 'Give this person a chance.' The Church remembers Barnabas as an apostle on 11 June.

talk: What does Barnabas mean?
How did Barnabas help Paul?
Who can you encourage today?
stories.prayer: Lord, make me an encourager. Amen.

vocab.means: to give someone courage or hope

stories.title: Nicholas and the Secret Gifts

text.4-6: Nicholas lived a long time ago, in a town called Myra. He loved God and he loved poor people. It is told that three sisters were very poor. They had no money for their future. At night, Nicholas put gold through their window. He did it three nights in a row. He did not want anyone to know it was him. Nicholas became a bishop, and children still remember him.
text.7-9: Nicholas was born in the town of Patara, in the land of Lycia, which is now part of Turkey. He became a monk, and he was chosen as archbishop of Myra, a very important bishop. Saint Nicholas was known for helping those who were in need. The old Lives of the Saints tell how three young women were so poor that they were in danger of coming to harm. Nicholas heard about it. On three nights in a row, he secretly passed gold through their window, enough to give each sister something to live on. All three were able to marry. Many years after he died, his body was taken to the city of Bari in Italy, and many people visit him there. He has long been remembered as a friend of children.
text.10-12: We do not have much that is certain about Nicholas. Butler, in his Lives of the Saints, says that all accounts agree he was from Patara and that he became bishop of Myra, and that the story of the three sisters is one of the things 'related' about him. This is how an old story is told: with care, and without claiming more than we know. What the story shows is a way of giving that Jesus teaches in the Sermon on the Mount: 'When you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.' The Santa Claus of our own time grew from the memory of this kind bishop. His feast day is 6 December.

talk: Why did Nicholas give the gold in secret?
What do you think the sisters felt when they found the gold?
What is a kind thing you could do without telling anyone?
stories.prayer: Saint Nicholas, friend of children, pray for us. Teach us to give quietly and gladly. Amen.

vocab.means: a leader who looks after the Church in a region

stories.title: Martin Shares His Cloak

text.4-6: Martin was a young soldier. One cold winter day he was riding in the city of Amiens. A poor man stood by the gate, shivering. He had almost no clothes. Many people walked past. Martin had no money with him. So he took his sword and cut his cloak in two. He gave half to the poor man. That night Martin dreamed of Jesus wearing the half-cloak. Martin was baptised soon after.
text.7-9: Martin became a soldier in the Roman army. Even before he was baptised, he was known as a kind and patient young man. One day in the middle of a hard winter, he was marching with other soldiers. At the gate of the city of Amiens, he met a poor man who was almost naked and shaking with cold. The man begged from everyone who passed, but nobody helped. Martin had nothing with him but his weapons and his cloak. So he drew his sword and cut the cloak in two. He gave one half to the beggar and wrapped himself in the other. Soon afterwards, Martin had a dream in which Jesus was wearing the half of the cloak. He was baptised, and later became bishop of Tours.
text.10-12: The story is told by Sulpicius Severus, who knew Martin, and it is repeated in Butler's Lives of the Saints. In the dream, Jesus says to the angels around him, 'Martin, who is still only a catechumen, has clothed me with this garment.' A catechumen is someone who is getting ready for baptism. Jesus has said something like this in the Gospel: 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me.' Martin was baptised in his eighteenth year. He shared what he had without making a fuss, and he gave half, not the whole, because it was half his. His feast is 11 November.

talk: Why did Martin give half of his cloak?
Who did Martin see in his dream?
What could you share with someone who has less?
stories.prayer: Saint Martin, pray for us. Help us to see Jesus in those who need our help. Amen.

vocab.means: a person preparing to be baptised

stories.title: Francis and the Man with Sores

text.4-6: Francis lived in Assisi in Italy. His father was a rich merchant, and Francis liked fine things. But God was calling him. One day Francis was riding and met a man with leprosy, a very bad skin disease. Francis was afraid. Then he got off his horse, gave the man money, and gave him a kiss. After that Francis loved to help sick and poor people. He gave up his money and lived simply.
text.7-9: Francis was born in Assisi, and his father was a rich cloth merchant. As a young man Francis was cheerful and generous, and he never turned away a poor person who asked for help. One day, riding on the plain near Assisi, he met a man with leprosy. At first Francis drew back in horror. Then he got down from his horse, gave the man an alms and kissed his sores with great tenderness. After that he often visited hospitals for lepers and served the sick. He heard a priest read the words of Jesus: do not take gold or silver or a bag for your journey. Francis took them as they were written. He gave away what he had and lived with very little. Other men joined him, and they became the Franciscans.
text.10-12: All of this comes from the old Life of Saint Francis summarised in Butler's Lives of the Saints. Butler says that Francis was moved by the story of the poor Christ in the stable at Bethlehem, and that he loved the feast of Christmas more than almost any other. He rebuilt a broken little church, San Damiano, with his own hands, carrying stones. Poverty for him was not sadness. It was a way of being free and of living like Jesus. At the end of the account, Butler adds that Francis thought of himself as very small. Saint Francis is remembered on 4 October,.

talk: What did Francis do when he met the man with leprosy?
Why did Francis give away what he owned?
What do you have that you could give away?
stories.prayer: Saint Francis, pray for us. Help me to love people who are poor or sick. Amen.

vocab.means: a skin disease that, long ago, made people afraid to go near

stories.title: Patrick Comes Back to Ireland

text.4-6: When Patrick was sixteen, robbers took him from his home. They carried him over the sea to Ireland, where he became a servant and looked after animals. He was cold and hungry. But Patrick prayed many times each day and each night. One night he had a dream telling him how to escape. He got home safely. Years later, he went back to Ireland to tell people about Jesus.
text.7-9: Patrick was born in Britain to a Christian family. In his sixteenth year, he was carried off by raiders and taken to Ireland as a slave. There he had to look after cattle on the mountains and in the forests, in hunger and cold, in snow, rain and ice. He wrote later that his faith grew stronger there. He prayed often in the day and many times in the night. After some time a dream told him to go home, and that a ship was ready. He escaped and returned to his family. But he felt that God was calling him back to Ireland. He became a bishop and, for about forty years, travelled across the island, preaching and baptising thousands.
text.10-12: The details here are taken from Butler's Lives of the Saints, which draws on Patrick's own writing, his 'Confession'. Patrick says he was not a learned man, and he took nothing from the many he baptised. He goes back to the land where he was a slave. That is a brave thing to do. He felt that God was calling him back to the people who had held him. The way in which Patrick teaches us is the way of the last words of Jesus in Matthew: 'Go and make disciples of all nations.' Saint Patrick's feast is 17 March. We do not know the exact dates of his life, and many stories about him, such as the shamrock, are not in the earliest sources.

talk: What happened to Patrick when he was sixteen?
Why did he go back to Ireland?
How can you forgive someone who has hurt you?
stories.prayer: Saint Patrick, pray for us. Help us to share our faith with kindness. Amen.

vocab.means: a leader who looks after the Church in a region

stories.title: Elizabeth Feeds the Hungry

text.4-6: Elizabeth was a princess in Hungary and Germany who loved Jesus. She prayed every day. She also used her money to help poor people. She gave them bread and clothes and built a hospital for the sick. She even looked after sick children and orphans. When she was a widow, she was treated unkindly, but she kept being kind. She spent her last years helping those in need.
text.7-9: Elizabeth was born in Hungary and was married as a young girl to Lewis, the ruler of Thuringia in Germany. Even as a young woman, she liked to pray. She seemed to know no better use of money than to give it to the poor. She spun coarse wool to make clothes for them. She built a hospital at the foot of the castle rock and cared for sick people there herself. She fed nine hundred people at her gate every day. After her husband died on his way to a Crusade, she was turned out of the castle. She went to live in poverty. A priest took her in, and she spent her last years in poverty, caring for those who were sick.
text.10-12: This account is based on Butler's Lives of the Saints. It says that Elizabeth's husband, who loved her, defended her when the servants complained about her giving. He said that her kindness to the poor would bring God's blessing on them all. The prophet Isaiah says that real worship means sharing your bread with the hungry, giving shelter to the poor and clothing the naked. Elizabeth did that, and she chose to do it herself, with her own hands, instead of sending others. The Church remembers her on 17 November. Many hospitals and charities carry her name.

talk: What did Elizabeth do for people in need?
Why do you think she did the work herself?
What can your family do to help people who are hungry?
stories.prayer: Saint Elizabeth, pray for us. Help us to share our food and our time. Amen.

vocab.means: a place where sick people are looked after

stories.title: Clare Chooses a Simple Life

text.4-6: Clare was born in Assisi. Her family was rich. When she heard Francis preach, she wanted to give her life to God. Francis cut her hair and gave her a plain dress. She went to live at San Damiano. She and her sisters lived simply and prayed a lot. Clare gave her money to the poor. Many other women joined her. They were known as the Poor Clares.
text.7-9: Clare was born in 1193 in Assisi, to a noble and wealthy family. She had heard Francis preach, and she asked to speak with him. She wanted to give her life to God. On Palm Sunday, she left her home in secret, and Francis cut off her hair and gave her a rough habit tied with a cord. Her family was upset and tried to bring her back, but she showed them her cut hair and said that Christ had called her. She went to live at the little church of San Damiano. Other women joined her, and she became their leader. When her father died, her large share of the family wealth came to her, and she gave it all to the poor.
text.10-12: This summary comes from Butler's Lives of the Saints. Butler says that Clare loved to be 'the servant of servants'. She washed the feet of the other sisters, served at table and looked after the sick. She spent many hours in prayer, and even when she was ill in bed she spun fine linen for church altars. Jesus said, 'Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.' Clare's treasure was God, and her life shows what that can mean. Her feast is 11 August. Her sisters, the Poor Clares, are still in many countries today.

talk: What did Clare give to the poor?
What did Clare want most?
What do you treasure most?
stories.prayer: Saint Clare, pray for us. Help me to love God more than things. Amen.

vocab.means: the simple clothes worn by monks and sisters
